### World economy suffering from crumbling brics – is more Qe the reQuired mortar? Brazil: Q2 GDP +0.8% year-on-year; july iP -5.5% yearon-year; july Pmi 48.7. peers, but how much does it really matter in the greater scheme of things? russia: Q2 GDP +4.0% y-o-y; july iP +3.4% y-o-y; july Pmi 52.0. india: Q1 GDP +5.3% y-o-y; june iP -1.2% m-o-m; july Pmi 52.9. china: Q2 GDP +7.6% y-o-y; july iP +9.2% y-o-y; july Pmi 49.3. The above is hardly an inspiring set of (selected) economic indicators, especially when viewed in the context of their generally declining performance and of previous market expectations. it has been evident for some time now that the travails faced by the mature economies, especially the eurozone and to a somewhat lesser extent, the united states, have not left the “saviour” Bric countries unscathed. china remains the giant amongst the fold, but even the mighty dragon has seen its wings clipped in recent months. slowing GDP and industrial production growth have been joined by a plethora of other less than sanguine indicators, including retail sales, inflation and new loans (see this and last months’ economic indicators sections for more detail). The chinese government has refrained from a third consecutive month of interest rate cuts, so far, but despite these being viewed (not too long ago) as a l

ast resort measure, surely more (and further reductions in banks’ reserve ratios) must be on the way? Brazilian growth prospects have diminished dramatically, while india has proven that it is nowhere close to being “the next china” – it is indeed struggling to remain the old india! russia has held up reasonably well compared to its The Brazilian government recently announced stimulus measures to provide up to Brl133 billion (us$66 billion) in private investment for road and rail projects. The country is already reported to be struggling to upgrade its infrastructure ahead of both the World cup and olympics, which it is hosting in 2014 and 2016, respectively. in an effort to revitalise growth prospects, the government has cut interest rates to an all-time low of 8% (and further cuts are expected imminently), while also providing consumers and industry with tax breaks and promising to increase government purchases of industrial goods. metaphorically, the lumbering elephant appears to have got stuck in the mud. indian industrial output fell for the third time in four months in june and the economy is in its worst slowdown in a decade. The country’s interest rates are amongst the highest of the major economies, but the reserve Bank of india has signalled that any cuts would only follow a reduction in inflation. This stance may come under pressure as GDP growth falters and government policy deters foreign investment. chinese policymakers’ fears over an economy growing out of control, and over the creation of housing and industryspecific “bubbles”, may be waning. We have previously noted the sharp slowdown in GDP growth, while industrial production has also decelerated. credit is the lifeblood of any economy, and certainly of commodity trading, but new yuan-based loans have slowed sharply. has the government been too successful in cooling the economy, just at the point when it needs to turn it around? ##### economic indicAToRS The overall oecD indicator, an important forward-looking gauge for metal markets, was revised marginally higher for may, to 100.4, leaving it unchanged since February. however, the june indicator fell slightly, to 100.3. The eurozone indicator is continuing a decline seen since january, and the two main economies of France and Germany both edged lower in june. The us and japanese indicators also declined from their may levels, whilst the Brics’ indicators were steady to lower (Brazil and china in the former category and india and russia in the latter). Whilst consumer confidence in most major economies has continued to fall, the united states confidence indicator bucked the trend, posting its first rise since February. it rose to 65.9 in july, from 62.7 the previous month. eurozone confidence, understandably, continued to slide, as did that for Brazil. Notably, having risen consecutively for the past three months, japanese confidence edged lower in july too. china’s latest consumer confidence indicator, for june, fell sharply, from 104.2 to 99.3, having risen in the previous two months. interestingly, the main purchasing managers’ indices that we highlight were mixed in july, having all fallen since April. The ism index for the united states edged fractionally higher in july to 49.8, having fallen sharply in june. however, this still showed a contraction in factory activity, when the market had generally

expected a return to expansion (i.e. a number over 50). The forward-looking new orders component rose to 48.0 in july, but was still low on a historical basis. exports, meanwhile, fell for a third consecutive month, to 46.5. The employment component, having held up reasonably well in june, sank to 52.0, from 56.6 the previous month. The eurozone Pmi fell to 44.0 in july (from 45.1 in june) and the japanese index fell to 47.9 (from 49.9). however, china’s Pmi, whilst still in contractionary territory, rebounded from 48.2 to 49.3. eurozone industrial production growth was revised higher for may, from 0.6%, month-on-month, to 0.9%. however, june saw negative growth, falling by 0.6%. The major economies all fared badly: French iP was flat in june, but monthly declines were seen in Germany, italy and the uK of 0.9%, 1.4% and 2.5%, respectively. us industrial production, meanwhile, grew at the fastest pace since April. may’s number was adjusted up, from -0.2% to +0.1%, whilst growth for june was revised down from 0.4% to 0.1%. however july’s iP came in at a better-thanexpected 0.6%. Within the total, factory production was up 0.5% in the month while utilities output bounced back from -3.3% in june to +1.3%. us capacity utilisation also rose from 78.9% to 79.3%. chinese indicators remained broadly negative. chinese industrial production fell to 9.2% year-on-year in july, from 9.5%, once again below consensus. contributing to this decline were sharp falls in industrial exports, the transport equipment industry and motor vehicle production (excluding cars). Fixed asset investment, meanwhile, remained unchanged through july, at 20.4%. Further highlighting the slowing economy was another fall in inflation in july (from 2.2% to 1.8%); lower retail sales growth (down from 13.7% to 13.1%) and a fall in new loans (from rmB919.8 billion to rmB540.1 billion). The indian economy also continues to disappoint. With first quarter 2012 GDP slumping to 5.3% from 9.2% in the previous quarter, more recent data continue to point to a difficult road ahead. industrial production slumped -1.2%, month-on-month, in june, having increased 3.5% in may. ###### market background the broader macro environment continues to disappoint, even with the recent “surprise” in German and french second quarter Gdp numbers, which were better than generally expected. this continues to weigh on the industrial metals complex, including aluminium. continued strong primary production growth in china, coupled with a weakening economic outlook for the nation, is a particular issue. however, given that aluminium prices have pushed further below their marginal costs, and certainly when viewed relative to other base metals, further downside risk looks to have been somewhat lessened (although this would probably depend on increased reaction by producers to curtail production). Indeed, during the month of July, the aluminium price was one of the better performers amongst the lme metals, losing only 1.2%. however, for the year to date, it has been the second-worst performing metal (the title goes to nickel), down by around 9% at the time of writing. ###### reported stocks show gains in July the declining trend in lme aluminium stocks, seen since february, has seen a partial reversal in recent weeks. having reached a nadir of 4.800 million tonnes in midJuly, inventories have subsequently edged higher (adding almost 56,000 tonnes in July alone) to 4.897 million tonnes, still well below the peak of 5.126 million. over the year to date, stocks have fallen by around 82,000 tonnes. detroit and vlissingen continue to dominate overall holdings of aluminium, and especially cancelled stocks. although cancelled warrants as a ratio of the total have actually edged lower as stocks built up recently, they still remain around at around 35%. meanwhile offtake queues continue to imply delivery dates pushing into april/may of next year from these locations. ###### weekly chanGe In lme stocks vs spot prIce 60000 2300

restricting the uptick in refined metal stocks.
